title: What Happens When You Press Enter on Google?
sources: Google, 'How Search organizes information' (the Search index contains hundreds of billions of webpages and is well over 100,000,000 GB)
Google, 'How Search works' (Search looks through its index, not the live web, and ranks results by relevance and usefulness)
Jeff Dean (Google), WSDM 2009 keynote, reported by Labnol / Gizmodo / Gigazine: a single query uses about 1,000 machines and returns in about 0.2 seconds
Cloudflare Learning Center, 'What is DNS?' (DNS turns a domain name into an IP address; data travels as packets)

lines.text: What happens when you press Enter on Google?
First, your browser asks a DNS server where Google lives,
lines.caps: YOUR *BROWSER | ASKS A *DNS SERVER | WHERE *GOOGLE LIVES

lines.text: and gets back a number called an IP address.
lines.caps: GETS BACK A *NUMBER | CALLED AN *IP ADDRESS

lines.text: Then your search zips off in tiny packets
to a nearby Google data center.
But Google doesn't search the live internet.
It searches its own giant index,
a copy of hundreds of billions of pages.
Up to a thousand computers team up on your one question,
lines.caps: UP TO *1,000 | *COMPUTERS | *TEAM UP ON | YOUR ONE *QUESTION

lines.text: and rank the matches by how useful they are.
Then the results fly back to your screen
in about two tenths of a second.
So every time you hit Enter,
you wake up a thousand computers.
